newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan March jobless rate at 2.79 percent.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan March jobless rate at 2.79 percent.

text.p: Taiwan's unemployment rate was at 2.79 percent in March, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said on Wednesday.
At 2.79 percent, the jobless rate for March came in slightly below an average forecast of 2.9 percent compiled in an April 18 Reuters poll of Taiwan economists.
Economists had said they expected the jobless rate in March to ease slightly from February as workers who changed jobs around Chinese new year (on February 7) gradually found new jobs in March.
Taiwan's enterprises usually pay bonuses days before the Chinese new year, and workers who want to quit typically would stay on until after they receive the bonuses.
The number of unemployed people in March decreased 16,000 to 262,000 from February. The number of employed increased 45,000 to 9.123 million.
Cheng Shuo-liang, a directorate section-chief, told reporters he expected jobless rate to climb in April due to an island-wide outbreak of hog foot-and mouth disease.
"The hog disease's impact on jobless rate will start to show in April," Cheng said. "But we cannot predict how serious it will be and how long it will last."
The directorate had said about 100,000 people would lose their jobs due to the epidemic, which triggered a March 20 ban on pork exports, bringing April's jobless rate to above 3.0 percent.
Taiwan lifted the export ban on April 17, but major importing countries, including Japan and Korea, have maintained their own ban on Taiwan pork.
Taiwan's jobless rate hovered close to 1.5 percent from 1991-1994, rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and pushed above 3.0 percent from August to October of 1996 before coming back down.
The jobless rate was 2.60 percent for all of 1996.

Officials had attributed the shift to higher jobless levels to a fundamental change in Taiwan's economy -- a broad move toward service-oriented industries from labour-intensive manufacturing that had powered the island's dramatic economic development.
